title_en: The Confluence of Maya and Brahman
translation:
Before beginning the Samagam, the purpose with which it was written is stated at the outset: ‘This Samagam has been written having seen the dharma [teaching/religion] of Namdev Kabirji.’ Thus the intent of writing this Samagam is to establish the dharma of Namdev Kabirji. Regarding Namdev Kabir, the Revered Yadunath Maharaj has explained the meaning as follows: Kabir and Namdev are not two persons — I interpret it to mean ‘Name itself is God’ (Nam j Dev). The meaning of Namdev is not the one from Panḍharpur in the south. Namdev: he for whom the Name alone is the chosen ideal is Kabir. The answers he gave to questions asked by devotees are as follows.

Question: What is this distinction between Maya and Brahman?

Answer: Know that to consider Maya and Brahman as separate is a mistaken view — this is Kabirji's own word. Maya and Brahman are one and the same. Just as there is no real difference between ice and water, there is no difference between the Formless (Nirgun) and the Manifest-with-attributes (Sagun). Maya is itself a form of the Supreme Being.

Question: What is the meaning of Namdev Kabir?

Answer: Devotees are of two kinds — one type gives primacy to the Name and then to the Form, the other gives primacy to the Form and then to the Name. If you paste a photograph on an envelope and post it, it will not reach the person; only if you write the name and address will it reach. In the same way, one who gives importance to the Name and honours the glory of the Name is called Namdev Kabir.

_Sumaran marag sahajka hai, sadguru diya batay ||
Shvase shvase sumartan, ek din milse aay ||1||_
(The path of remembrance is the natural, easy path — the true Guru has shown it. Remembering with every breath, one day you will surely attain union.)

Question: What is the dharma of Namdev Kabir?

Answer: The dharma of Namdev Kabir is, in effect, a great covenant. This dharma is very expansive — a dharma of pure devotion (bhakti) filled with extremely profound intentions. No procedure of mantra or ritual sadhana enters into it. It is not the threefold (trigun) devotion associated with Aumkar, but a distinct dharma that displays the fourth, transcendent devotion beyond the three gunas, symbolized by the double-ring (rankari) sound. It stands untouched by Maya and Brahman [in the ordinary sense]. It is free from vices, misconduct, and the like. Even its speech and manner of expression are unique. In this dharma there is true and sincere devotion to the Guru, devotion free of hypocrisy, deceit, ritualism, and sacrificial rites (yajna); and it also incorporates the distinct devotion drawn from the essence of the fourteen kinds of the higher dharma. In short, the dharma that rescues us from the snare of the merchant-thief who, in the name of Vishnu-bhakti, diverts us from single-minded devotion and leads us onto the path of ritual works, and shows us instead the path of true, loving devotion — that is the dharma of Namdev Kabir. The dharma that warns us not to be deceived in the name of liberation through japa, austerity, and the like — that is the dharma of Namdev Kabir.

**He came for the welfare of His own people**

The true Guru (Sadguru) desires the welfare of everyone, but for those who do not take refuge in the Sadguru, the Sadguru is helpless [to do more].

_Sai ye shabda pukariya, tun sun re Jivandas ||
Nij jankun parmodh ke, lavo hamare paas ||2||_
(The Lord called out this word: ‘Listen, O Jivandas! Instruct My own people and bring them to Me.’)

_Ek achamba esa sunya, hiro haat bekay ||
Parakhnaro andhalo, kodi badle jaay ||3||_
(I have heard of a strange wonder: a diamond is sold in the marketplace, but the appraiser is blind, so it goes for the price of a mere cowrie shell.)

_Hiro aavyo haathmen, samjavyo so vaar ||
Kahet Kabir aave nahi, andheko mat saar ||4||_
(The diamond came into hand and was explained a hundred times over, says Kabir, yet the blind one does not understand — he cannot grasp its true worth.)

_Tran lokman Jamra raja bhaya, ankush bandhya dwaar ||
Shabda hamaro maanse, betha Jamra roy ||5||_
(In the three worlds Yamraj has become king, binding a restraining hook at every door; but whoever obeys my word — before that word — Yamraj sits and weeps, helpless.)

_Matha vinana maanvi, suniyo Jivandas ||
Nij bhagat parmodhke, lavo hamare paas ||6||_
(O fearless ones, listen, Jivandas! Instruct My own devotees and bring them to Me.)

_Jivan kahe men bohot kari, laaye the Brahm ghaat ||
Sabahi bhoole bhekhmen, koi gafave vaat ||7||_
(Jivan says: I made many efforts and brought them to the shore of Brahman, but all get lost in false disguises — someone leads them astray on the path.)

_Jivanku je jan mile, sohi utre paar ||
Dooja e paate haar gaye, bhavsagarke haat ||8||_
(Whoever meets and joins with Jivan crosses over; all the others lose out and remain caught in the marketplace of the ocean of worldly existence.)

_Jine Jivan jaanya nahin, taaka koti paat ||
Dharam raayke chotare, Jam khele jan ||9||_
(Whoever has not known Jivan will undergo crores of births; at the court of Dharamraj, Yam torments such a soul.)

_Je Jivanka hoyga, boojega vichaar ||
Jesa sunmen jai bhale, baaro maas khelat ||10||_
(Whoever becomes Jivan's own will awaken to right understanding, and will dwell joyfully in that emptiness the whole year round.)

_Van govale Jivana, dhor gaye sab fel ||
Laathi le Sadguru khada, so laaye apne gel ||11||_
(O Jivan, without a cowherd, the cattle have all scattered and strayed; the Sadguru stands with his staff and brings them back to his own fold.)

_Andekhi an sambhli, Sadguru deve saakh ||
Ab nidra kyon sove Jivana, naam nirmal jas gaay ||12||_
(Of what has never been seen or heard, the Sadguru gives testimony; so why, O Jivan, do you still sleep in slumber? Now sing the pure glory of the Name.)

_Deepak dekhya Jivana, Sadguru shabda parmaan ||
Shabdano otho andhaar, karam dharamki haat ||13||_
(O Jivan, I have seen the lamp — the Sadguru's word is the proof; but when the word gets shrouded, darkness comes — that is the marketplace of ritual works and religion.)

_Shabda vichari jo chale, guru mukh nihaar ||
Kaam krodh vyape nahin, kaal kabhu na khaay ||14||_
(Whoever walks reflecting on the Word, looking to the Guru's guidance, is never overcome by lust and anger, and death never devours him.)

_Shabdake maarya mar gaya, shabde chhodya raaj ||
Jine shabda pichaniya, taaka sariya kaaj ||15||_
(Struck by the Word, he died to the self; for the Word's sake he gave up his kingdom; whoever has recognized the Word, his purpose has been accomplished.)

_Raam baith vicharya, saakhi kaho Kabir ||
Bhavsagarman doobtan, koik paave teer ||16||_
(Ram sat and reflected, and told Kabir this couplet: among those drowning in the ocean of worldly existence, perhaps someone will reach the shore.)

_Je Jivanka hoega, paavega nij gyaan ||
Parbrahm pad cheen kari, laage nishchal dhyaan ||17||_
(Whoever becomes Jivan's own will attain true self-knowledge; recognizing the state of the Supreme Brahman, he becomes fixed in unwavering meditation.)

_Kabir dharti to handi bhai, dhankan bhaya aakash ||
Chaar Ved kaathi bhai, jeevka kahan nikaash ||18||_
(Kabir says: the earth, the body, has become a cooking-pot, the sky has become its lid, the four Vedas have become the firewood burning beneath it — where, then, will the soul find escape?)

_Kabir dharti to handi sahi, dhankan sahi aakash ||
Sadguru shabda bhakt pichaniya, jeevka tahan nikaash ||19||_
(Kabir says: yes, the earth is indeed the pot and the sky indeed the lid, but the devotee who has recognized the Sadguru's Word — for him, even from this pot, is the soul's escape.)

_Tab bole Hari Rai Gusai, karm kaand tum deho bahai ||
Tumaaro shabda sune je koi, toko janm maran nahin hoi ||20||_
(Then the Lord, the great Master, spoke: ‘You shall sweep away ritualism. Whoever hears your Word shall not undergo birth and death.’)

_Jahan tum hi tahan hame, hame tahan tum hoy ||
So nishche kar raakhahi, paarahi pahoche soy ||21||_
(Where you are, there am I; where I am, there you shall be — whoever holds this certainty firmly shall reach the far shore.)

The Lord called out and, giving a command, addressed Jivanji Maharaj thus: ‘O Jivandas! Listen — instruct My own worthy devotees and bring them to Me’ — (2).

When the Lord commanded Jivandas, the resident of Vrindavan, to give true instruction to His own people and send them to Us, Jivandasji said: ‘I feel great astonishment — the priceless diamond that is human birth is sold in the marketplace of the eighty-four lakh species in exchange for trivial sensory desires. Such are the people, blind with sense-attachment, who fail to recognize the worth of human birth’ — (3).

Even one such as Kabir made attempts hundreds of times to make human society understand, yet those blinded by sensory desire do not find right understanding — (4).

Therefore the sovereign rule of Yamraj prevails throughout the three worlds. He binds everyone in the noose of Yama and drags them to his door. But whoever heeds my counsel — before them, Yamraj's power will not prevail — (5).

So, O Jivandasji, whatever devotees have the courage to struggle against Maya or against worldly people, even to the point of death, without any care for it — such of your most devoted, wholly-surrendered servants, instruct them and bring them to Me — (6).

Jivandasji says: I made great efforts and brought them right up to the landing-place of devotion, but disguised impostors mislead some of them into their snares and secretly divert them from the path of devotion — (7).

But those who remained faithfully attached to Jivanji Maharaj crossed over the ocean of worldly existence; all the rest fell into the grip of the traffic of that ocean — (8).

Thus those who have not known and not understood Jivanji Maharaj must go through crores of births and deaths; they suffer torment in the court of Yamraj — (9).

Those who take refuge in Jivanji Maharaj and accept his teaching will merge into the divine reality and attain eternal happiness — (10).

Without the Sadguru as their cowherd, guru-less people wander here and there like stray cattle, but the Sadguru, with the staff of true teaching, turns them back and brings them onto the path of devotion — (11).

The Sadguru shows us and makes us understand a teaching of true devotion such as we had never had the chance to hear before. So, having come to know this, why should we be lazy in practicing devotion? We ought now to devote ourselves to the pure praise of Ramkabir — (12).

I have seen the Sadguru's instructive words as a lamp casting authentic light, but when the covering of the business of ritualistic religious words comes over it, darkness comes in the form of deviation from the path of devotion — (13).

But if one understands the Sadguru's words and walks following the Guru's teaching as a guru-facing disciple, no onslaught of lust, anger, and the like will come upon him; nor can death ever do him any harm — (14).

Those upon whom the true Word has had a decisive effect have offered up even their very life-breath; they have renounced the splendours of kingdom and throne. Thus those who have understood the true Word have accomplished their purpose — (15).

Ram, sitting at ease, having understood and reflected, commanded Kabir to speak true words, so that among the people drowning in the ocean of worldly existence, some might be able to cross that ocean — (16).

Whoever takes refuge in Jivanji Maharaj will become aware of his own true welfare, and, having understood the reality of the Supreme Being, will thereafter engage in unwavering remembrance of Him — (17).

Then Kabir said: ‘O Lord! Listen — there is one thing I cannot bear: that people caught up in ritualism will not accept what I say.’ Kabir went on to say: the body, made of the five elements arising from the four wombs, is like a pot set upon the earth, and the sky — meaning the state of residence in the womb — is its tightly fastened lid, and beneath it the four Vedas, like firewood, have been set ablaze — so from such a bondage, where will the soul find deliverance?’ — (18).

Kabirji then explains: yes, the body made of the five elements is indeed the earthen pot, and yes, the residence in the womb is indeed the lid — but those souls who will have understood the Sadguru's teaching and clung to devotion, they will be able to escape from it — (19).

At that the Lord said: ‘You shall be able to pull away the firewood that is the Vedas of ritualism; therefore whoever accepts your words will not have to undergo birth and death’ — (20).

‘Wherever you are, there I am; and wherever I am, there you shall be.’ Whoever holds such faith will be able to reach across the ocean of worldly existence — (21).

_Ram satya | Naam satya | Shri Guru sat chhe |_
‘Ram (Naam) is Truth’ — here the word ‘Ram’, used in the sense of ‘Naam’ (the Name), is applied to mean the Supreme Being, Parabrahma.

The custom of writing ‘Ramkabir is Truth’ is very widespread in our community. In Surat district in particular, it is written on almost every house. In America too, these words are printed on golden posters and distributed among devotees. I too have received stickers from there.

In Vishnu-bhakti there is a great confluence (bhel) of Maya and Brahman.

This confluence pervades the entire cosmos, and because of it a great confusion prevails over how the soul is to cross beyond it. Therefore no one in the three worlds has the power to understand the workings — the intricate entanglement — of this Maya-Brahman. So the Lord sent one such as Narad to Brahma to obtain clarification.

Naradji is a devotee, and a man of knowledge (gyani); therefore he goes about carrying Saraswati's instrument, the veena. Moreover, a man of knowledge always retains a longing to attain complete knowledge, and so wanders throughout the whole world. Thus Naradji wanders about carrying Saraswati's veena, yet cannot arrive at a resolution of the puzzle of Maya and Brahman. Nor can the three great gods (Tridev) or Saraswati bring about its resolution. Naradji is called a muni (sage); the definition of a muni is as follows:

_Atmaramo hi santushto nirdwandva shitalashaya: |
Nirmohi nirahankaro prabudha: samadrig muni: ||
Dwai padam cha chatushpadam padam bahu padakam |
Sarvatra nitya chidrupam pashyate muni: ||1||_
(A muni is one who remains absorbed only in self-knowledge and self-contemplation, content, free of dualities such as pleasure and pain, wishing harm to no one, free of delusion, free of ego, gentle, and even-visioned. He who looks upon all — two-legged, four-legged, or many-legged beings — everywhere and always as pure consciousness is called a muni.)

Naradji is called a muni, but he is also reckoned a Devarshi (divine sage), and so he keeps wandering caught in the clash between the path of knowledge and the path of devotion. Kabirji has indeed said, regarding this:

_Man re te bhajyana Raghupati Raja, tathe saryona eku kaja ||tek||
Charo Ved padhya mukh apno, kari karam ki aasha |
Graase kaal sab lok sayana, Brahma chale re niraasa ||1||_
(O mind, you have not worshipped Raghupati Raja — hence not one of your tasks has been accomplished. You recited all four Vedas with your own mouth, hoping thereby for good deeds, yet time devours all these wise people; even Brahma departs disappointed.)

_Ved Puran padho mat gaao, inhunmen kinhu na paaya |
Sandhya tarpan or khat karma, inhu the agam bataaya ||2||_
(Do not read or sing the Vedas and Puranas — no one has found anything in them. Evening rites, water-offerings, and the six duties — none of these has shown the way to the Unfathomable.)

_Ban khand jaay jog tap kina, kandmool khani khaaya |
Pandit guni sur kavi daata, Jamke pate lakhaaya ||3||_
(They went into the forest and performed yoga and austerity, digging up and eating roots and tubers; yet pandits, virtuous men, gods, poets, and the generous alike — all have their names recorded on Yama's register.)

_Narade bhagat harde nahin jaani, naach kaachh chit dina |
Raag ragini dambar kapat kari, une Haripe kaha lina ||4||_
(Narad did not truly know devotion in his heart; he gave his attention to dance and celibate discipline. Through melody and tune, pomp and deceit, what did he really gain from the Lord?)

_Petho kaal trahe lok upar, beech lakhe Brahmagyani |
Kahe Kabir jan bhaye khalsa, Ram bhagat jine jaani ||5||_
(Time has taken hold over all three worlds; among them are counted even those who call themselves knowers of Brahman. Kabir says: only those devotees become truly pure and free who have known devotion to Ram.)

Meaning: O mind! You have not worshipped Raghupati Ram, and therefore not one of your undertakings will succeed. Though you recited the four Vedas with your own mouth in hope of religious merit, even such learned people are devoured by time. Even Brahma, disappointed, passes into the jaws of time. Therefore do not merely read or chant the Vedas and Puranas — no one has gained anything from that. The evening prayers, water-libations, and the six ritual duties cannot lead one to attain the reality of God. Yogis go into the forest, perform austerities, and dig up and eat roots and tubers; yet pandits, virtuous men, gods, poets, and the charitable are all likewise entered in Yama's register. Even Narad did not know true devotion within his heart. He directed his attention to dance, song, and celibacy, and by singing in various melodies practiced hypocrisy, pretense, and deceit among people — but what did he actually gain from God through that? Time has become sovereign over all three worlds, and among those recorded in its register are even such knowers of Brahman as Narad. Kabirji says: O devotees! Only those who have known devotion to Ram remain exempt from this time.

Because of this confluence of Maya and Brahman, a net of difficulties descends upon anyone practicing Vishnu-bhakti. One gets entangled in the temptations of ritualism, the path of knowledge, the path of yoga, and so on, and thereby obstacles arise in Vishnu-bhakti. The net of Maya is extremely hard to escape. As regards Maya, there is a place of pilgrimage called Haridwar, whose other names are Hardwar, Gangadwar, and Mayadwar. One mile above Hardwar, on the right bank of the Ganga, is a village called Mayapuri, where there are three temples: (1) of Mayadevi, (2) of Bhairav, and (3) of Narayan. The image of Mayadevi has three heads and four arms. Nearby is an image of Shiva with seven arms. In Indian society, the images made of the various gods and goddesses are shaped to convey the particular characteristics of each deity. This image of Mayadevi is of a strange kind; likewise Shivji having seven arms also shows something unusual. Yogmaya has eight arms, as though representing the eight limbs of yoga. But Maya is deceptive by nature, and this strangeness of hers is not something that can be fully understood — such confusing of the intellect is Maya's very quality.

Naradji — the son of Brahma, thirsting for knowledge, carrying Saraswati's instrument, wandering the three worlds out of longing for the path of devotion, stirring restlessness in everyone's mind and spreading an atmosphere of discord — this Naradji, Vasudev sends to Brahmaji, who is proud both of his status as Brahma and of being the creator of the universe. The Brahman-knowing and outspoken Naradji, without any regard for the dignity of Brahmaji, who has himself called self-born (Swayambhu), addressed him instead as Kamalbhu (lotus-born) and asked: ‘O Kamalbhu! On what authority do you claim to be the creator of this universe? You yourself are lotus-born, not self-born.’ There is a deliberate intent behind asking in this pointed manner: since you yourself have manifested out of a lotus, first go and find your own origin.

The idea has taken hold in people's minds throughout the world that we ought to know the Self (atma), and so they make futile efforts to attain self-knowledge. Brahmaji himself went down the stalk of the lotus from which he had originated for a thousand years, yet could not find its end. And Brahmanical tradition instituted the custom of gotra (lineage), making everyone declare which gotra they come from. When even a figure like Brahma has not attained his own root, the Brahmins still make vain attempts to show us our root in the name of our gotra. No one has yet truly ripened into a knower of the Self. Yet people of the world, growing utterly infatuated over self-knowledge, insist on taking refuge in learned, Brahman-established gurus in order to obtain self-knowledge.

The Revered Yadunath Maharaj has written, with reference to the dialogue between Narad and Brahma, that although Brahman has no desire, the world has nevertheless come into being. As evidence for this, following the Vedanta, proofs of inertness (jadatva) are conceived of as residing in Maya. The world is not ultimately real. Even though Brahman is inactive, it is said in the Gita that, under My governance, Maya gives birth to the world. Because of the Lord's divine play (lila), the Supreme Being, Parabrahma, is the creator of the world; and Yadunath Maharaj cites the Gita on this point as well. But this cannot be explained by gods such as Brahma or Shiva — Vasudev has entangled these proud gods in a knot they cannot undo.

The working of the world has been carried on with the support of the five elements and the three gunas; these lines from Kabir's Ramaini have been presented in this Samagam:

_Panch tattva trigun, sakat kari saniya_
(the five elements and three gunas — He fashioned and set them in place by His power).

The Revered Yadunath Maharaj states that, regarding garbhadhyan (contemplation in the womb), in the seventh month within the mother's womb the soul recalls the deeds it performed in its past, and its true original form also becomes visible to it. This is called garbhadhyan; this account is found in the Bhagavat.

The Samagam of Shri Guru Jivandasji: he came for the welfare of his own people, his own children. Ram (the Name) is Truth.

First: for the Vishnu-bhakta, there is a great confluence (bhel) of Maya and Brahman. ‘Bhel’ means union, combination (mixture, impurity) — Amaigamation Combination — not that the two are completely merged, reflecting fully into one another, but rather, within the embodied soul (jivatma), both Maya and Brahman, through a combining of their reflected influence — through this union of the two — the entire universe is pervaded. So how, then, is the soul to cross beyond it? (It is exactly this question on which this scripture has been composed.) In the three worlds, where all is a moving process whose death is certain, who is capable of knowing it? Here the word ‘ko’ is used in the sense of ‘who’, and should not be taken to mean ‘anyone at all.’ The question asked here — who is capable — uses the word in the sense of a specific count [i.e. referring to a defined list]; this list is given in a later chapter. That confusion pervades the universe. For this reason Vasudevji sent Narad Muni to Brahma. This Naradji said to Brahma: ‘O Kamalbhu! You who arose from a lotus — on what basis do you hold this claim to be the part that creates this universe? How do you claim to be the creator of the universe?’ Naradji spoke further: ‘O Brahma! Desire cannot arise in Brahman — if desire could arise, how could it be called Brahman? Where no desire can arise, that is called inert (jad) Brahman. Maya, too, is unconscious. If Maya were conscious, she would be called mighty. Maya is not conscious. Therefore she only generates — that is, produces, gives birth to — and equally causes to perish.’ That is to say, Maya performs the function of a catalyst in the work of creating the universe. Maya is inert and unconscious; and yet, through contact with conscious Brahman, creation occurs. Maya functions as an intermediary or broker — for which the Samagam uses the specific word ‘upaje’ (arises, is produced).

_Maya hyesha maya srishta yanmam pashyasi Narada ||
Sarvabhutagunairyuktam naivam mam jnatumarhasi ||2||_
(Mahabharat, Shanti Parva, ch. 339, shlok 45)
(This, O Narada, which you see as Me endowed with the qualities of all beings, is the Maya created by Me — you ought not to know Me merely in this way.)

Narayan said to Naradji: ‘O Narad, that which you behold as Me, endowed with all divine qualities, is the Maya fashioned by Me. It is not fitting for you to know Me only in this way.’

This exposition is explained by way of a corroborating statement — a reliable, trustworthy illustration — namely, Kabirji's couplet, in the metre of Rekhta:

_Panch tattva trigun, sakat kari saniya ||
Ashtvarn hot nahi, na karm kaya ||1||_
(variant reading: _Tan man hota na karm, beej kaya paap punya ||_)
(The five elements and the three gunas — He, by His power, fashioned and set them in place. The eight-fold [prakriti] did not yet exist, nor did karma or the body. Variant: Body and mind did not exist, nor karma; the seed-body of sin and merit did not yet exist.)

_Paap pun beej, ankor jaame mare ||
Vanse upje so, sarva maya ||2||_
(The seed of sin and merit sprouts and dies; whatever perishes and whatever arises — all of that is Maya.)

That is to say, the five elements are reckoned as belonging to Prakriti (material nature): earth, water, fire, air, and space; and the three gunas are sattva, rajas, and tamas. (The Revered Yadunathji Maharaj's commentary notes the three kinds of karma: prarabdha, kriyaman, and sanchit — accumulated, being performed, and stored — and the seed-body of sin and merit.) Before creation, the five elements and three gunas did not exist; ‘He fashioned and set them by His power’ — meaning the Lord established all of these by His own power.

(Ramkabir, dated 14-6-64, Sunday, Jeth Sud 5, Samvat 2020 — written by Brother Dwarkadas Gordhandas Bhagat, resident of Ghoda, Puniyad. Respectfully bound in loving attachment, from Y.J. At the beginning of the Ramkabir Samagam is written Kabirji's testimony:

_Panch tattva trigun, sakat kari saniya ||
Ashtvarn hot nahi, na karm kaya ||1||
Paap pun beej, ankor jaame mare ||_)

Regarding this, Naradji spoke, and with the thought of comparing the above words with Gita, chapter 7, verse 4, [Yadunath Maharaj] writes and sends the shloka along with its Hindi commentary, as follows:

_Bhoomirapo'nalo vayu: kham manobuddhireva cha ||
Ahankar itiyam me bhinna prakritirashtadha ||3||_ (Gita, ch. 7, v. 4)
(Meaning: O Arjuna, earth, water, fire, air, and space, as well as mind, intellect, and ego — these are the eight ways into which My material nature is divided.)

_Apareyamitastvanyam prakritim viddhi me param ||
Jeevabhootam mahabaho yayedam dharyate jagat ||4||_ (Gita, ch. 7, v. 5)
(This eightfold nature is the lower nature — that is, My inert, material nature. And, O mighty-armed one, know the other, distinct from this, to be My higher nature in the form of the individual soul — that is, the conscious nature — by which this entire universe is sustained.)

Kabirji states in the couplet that follows that the jivatma (soul) comes into the world of death and departs from it carrying its own karmas. Prakriti (Maya) clings to it in many forms. According to Yaskacharya's view, the states of the jivatma are as follows: jayate — to be born, aste — to remain, vardhate — to grow, viparinamate — to undergo change and alteration, kshayate — to decline, nashyate — to perish, to die. These are the six states of the jivatma. Every jivatma must settle the account of its karma right here in this world.

Kabirji identifies all of these matters as ‘Maya.’

So Naradji said: ‘O Brahma! Tell me one thing in detail — if Brahman is inert and Maya is unconscious, then how did this universe come into being? Explain this with an illustration.’ This puzzle — a problem requiring explanation with an example — this tangled riddle was presented at Narad's request to the Lord.

But Brahmaji could not give a correct answer to this doubt, so he sat down in meditation, and meditated for sixty thousand years. Then Mahadev Shankar came, and Yogmaya Parvati came with him; yet they too could not resolve Brahmaji's doubt. At that time Shri Vasudevji spoke, a voice from the sky: ‘O gods! You have come into being through Maya; therefore a womb-birth is possible for you — you must go through the cycle of birth and death. If you wish to be freed from this cycle of birth and death, take up garbhadhyan. But garbhadhyan will not come within your understanding — why is that? Because a union of Maya and Brahman has taken place in you.’ That is to say, among the Tridev (the three great gods) there is this confluence of Maya and Brahman — that is, in the Triveni, the threefold-gunas creation, among the Tridev: Parvati-Shiva, Ganga (of Shiva); Lakshmi-Narayan, Yamuna (of Vishnu); Brahmani-Brahma, Saraswati (of Brahma) — and the entire universe lies in the jaws of time. This universe is pervaded by the bondage of time, of birth and death. No one can escape from its snare. Only that jivatma can become free who has fixed his mind upon garbhadhyan.

Through the path of dhyan-yoga, Brahmaji, Shivji, and yogis alike strive to attain garbhadhyan and thereby know the hidden mystery of the world, but they have failed. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj speaks on this in the section on Garbhavali (the round of entering the womb):

_Garbhdhyan cheenho nahi, kare Harijansu vivaad ||
Ant bhandivaado Jivana, kaha raachyo anahad naad ||22||_
(Not having recognized garbhadhyan, one gets into disputes with the devotees of Hari; in the end, O Jivan, it comes to a potter's workshop — endless rounds of rebirth — why have you become so absorbed in the unstruck sound?)

Meaning: On the theme of Garbhavali — that is, the recurring tradition of entering and leaving the womb — Jivanji Maharaj says: even after performing worship rooted in Aumkar and the three gunas, one still has to enter and leave the womb. He has failed to understand this even by following the path of dhyan-yoga, and, taking the side of the path of dhyan-yoga, he began to oppose and dispute with those devotees who practice devotion to Hari. But your condition is like that of a potter in the potters' quarter shaping pots — you too will have to enter the wombs of the eighty-four lakh species. So why have you become so addicted to this path of dhyan-yoga and clung to the sound-Brahman?

_Aankh michine aandhalo, dhyan dhare aakash ||
Sitapati bhootal vase, jahan sant sangat nivaas ||23||_
(Closing his eyes like a blind man, he fixes his meditation upon the sky; but the Lord of Sita [Ram] dwells upon the earth, wherever the company of saints resides.)

Meaning: Jivanji Maharaj says that, like a blind man though having eyes, closing their eyes, yogis meditate upon Brahman thinking that Ram resides up in the sky. But Ram in fact dwells upon the earth, wherever the company of saints is found.

The wondrous design of God's creation cannot even be imagined; regarding this it is said:

_Aaspaas to safed hai, safed manhi ek shyaam ||
Shyaam manhi ek pootli, taame betha Raam ||24||_
(All around is white, and within the white is a black; within the black is a small pupil, and within that pupil sits Ram.)

Meaning: Around the eye's pupil there is a white colour; within that black pupil there is again a tiny pupil, through which everything can be seen. It seems as though within that pupil God Ram Himself dwells, working His marvel. Through black glass, black is seen; through red glass, red is seen; but through this wondrous black pupil, whatever is black is seen as black, whatever is red is seen as red — everything is seen as it truly is. Thus, though the pupil itself is black, only black is not all that is seen — what a marvel this is!

Kabir has described the dialogue in which Parvati asks a yogi such as Shiva about garbhadhyan:

_Swapna rahit nidra sukh saar, garbhdhyan ene aakaar ||
Chintavan man jaisa hoye, garbhdhyan kahiye soy ||25||_
(The essential joy of dreamless deep sleep — such is the form of garbhadhyan. Whatever state the mind is in when free of anxious thought — that is called garbhadhyan.)

_Jagat sesa kahiye teh, garbhdhyan uchit dhare jeh ||
Devi avastha nahi jehne, garbhdhyan kahiye tehne ||26||_
(He for whom the world is left behind as a mere remainder is the one who truly holds garbhadhyan. O Devi, he who has passed beyond any particular state — him alone is garbhadhyan to be called.)

_Sada nirantar sarkho jeh, kahiye naash na paame teh ||
Achhato ahankaar upaaye upaadh, Devi tahan nenan he samaadh ||27||_
(He who remains ever constant, always the same — of him it is said he never perishes; with the subtlest trace of ego removed by right effort, O Devi, his very eyes are in samadhi.)

_Kabir garbhdhyan gat upje, or khankhe sansaar ||
Man vichaar na kare, Hari nahi nirdhaar ||28||_
(Kabir says: when the true understanding of garbhadhyan arises, and one has cast off the world entirely, and the mind entertains no further thought — then Hari is not far to be attained.)

Kabir has written many couplets about garbhadhyan; here let us view just a few, with their meanings.

Meaning: O Parvati, just as the joy of deep, dreamless sleep, free of all manner of strange dreams, is experienced, in the very same way the experience of a structured joy occurs in garbhadhyan. Such a state of mind, free of all anxious thought, is called garbhadhyan. (25)

In dividing out the gunas, he for whom the world remains only as a remainder — he who becomes detached from the world — for him, it is said, true garbhadhyan has occurred. O Devi, for such a one, none of the states — waking, dream, deep sleep, the turiya state, or even beyond turiya — apply any longer; that is called garbhadhyan. (26)

That person is always, at all times, one and the same, unchanging; nothing in him ever perishes — the subtlest trace, hidden even in the finest degree, is removed through fitting effort so that not the least ego remains. O Devi, such a one's very eyes are truly established in samadhi. (27)

Kabirji says: those who have gained true understanding of garbhadhyan of this kind, and who have cast out worldly desire the way one spits out phlegm from the throat, and who no longer even entertain such thought in the mind — from such people God is certainly not far away; they are able to hold God within them. (28)

In addition to the words of the saints, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has offered proof-texts, citing shlokas from the Gita, the Bhagavat, the Adhyatma Ramayana, the Geet Govind, the Krishnakarnamrit composed by Lilashuk, the Gangashtak written by Shankaracharya, the Niranjan Purana, the Parashar Smriti, the Mahabharata, the Pandav Gita, the Garuda Purana, the Skanda Purana, the Narsinh Purana, the Padma Purana, the Ram Raksha Stotra, and other scriptures as well.

Brahma holds garbhadhyan, but he holds it only in order to trace the lineage of his hereditary gotra; and yet even he cannot discover where he himself came from. Meanwhile the Brahmins compel us to decide whether our lineage runs through the Kashyap gotra or some other gotra — but Brahma himself does not know where he came from, or in whose line he arose, and yet expects us to know our own clan and gotra: all of this is contrived. Likewise, Shivji, through Yogmaya, makes efforts toward garbhadhyan, but yogis have not been able to know the Supreme Reality. Thus, a verse from the Purana has been cited confirming that Shiva, Brahma, and the other gods too remain subject to time, caught in the cycle of birth and death. Such Puranas and scriptures are given the name ‘true scripture’ (sat shastra). Jivanji Maharaj does not accept every statement made in such scriptures and Puranas as valid, because ritualism, sacrificial rites, and practices of japa and austerity have also been smuggled into the Vedas, Puranas, and scriptures. So the scriptures have created a mixture of both the true and the false, and thereby introduced corruption; but Jivanji Maharaj points out whatever true statement exists within these Puranas, scriptures, and so on. Therefore, in this Samagam, whatever is beyond what Jivanji Maharaj himself has presented — however much more the scripture or Purana may say — all of that is not acceptable to us. Hence the meaning of ‘sat shastra’ is this: only whatever true statement exists within the scriptures should be understood as sat shastra — that is precisely why the term ‘sat shastra’ is used. Here, the first shloka is cited to show that the fact that Shiva, Brahma, and the other gods remain subject to time is stated in the Padma Purana. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj accepts the true fact contained within it and thereby makes it sat shastra. It is stated in Narad Bhakti Sutra 69:

_Tirthikurvanti tirthani, sukarmikurvanti karmani, sacchastrikurvanti shastrani ||69||_
(They make the places of pilgrimage into true pilgrimage, they make deeds into good deeds, and they make scriptures into true scripture.)

Such devotees turn places of pilgrimage into true pilgrimage sites, turn deeds into good deeds, and turn scriptures into true scripture.

_Kalai: sampoornasiddhi: syat, kalo mitrasya sangraha ||
Kalakaranamaruhya, kala: karoti peeditan ||1||_
(Complete accomplishment comes through time; through time, friends are gathered together. Mounted upon the cause that is time, time itself brings suffering upon people.)

Now the commentary: Shri Vasudev spoke thus: ‘O gods! You remain subject to time — that is, to birth and death! O gods, you keep time as though it were a friend; therefore all your deeds arise on account of time. Hence you remain resting in the very middle of the palm of time's hand’ — that is, whenever time wishes, you must go up and down through the cyclic maze of birth and death.

_Kala: srijati bhootani, kala: palayate praja ||
Kala: sangahate lokan, kalo'pi harate priyan ||2||_
(Time creates living beings; time nurtures its subjects; time gathers up the peoples of the world; and time carries off even our loved ones.)

Commentary: Shri Vasudev said — the world of beings, this physical universe, has come into existence through time. Time nurtures the entire universe physically; thus the universe is time's own offspring, its food. But for what reason does time undertake the task of destroying this creation? Such an effortless carrying out of the destruction of this creation ought to be difficult — yet here it is the reverse. By whose grace does this happen?

The 248th shloka in the first, introductory (Anukramanika) Parva of the Mahabharata pertains to this second verse.

_Kala: srijati bhootani, kala: sanharate praja: ||
Sanharantam praja: kalam, kala: shamayate puna: ||5||_
(Meaning: Time itself creates all beings, and time itself destroys all beings; but that time, which destroys all beings, is itself pacified by the Supreme Being in the form of Mahakaal.)

Just as a gardener comes into the garden, looks over the plants he has himself planted, and then picks whichever flowers and fruits please him and carries them away, so time carries off, at whatever moment it wishes, those jivatmas who remain subject to it. But if a jivatma has instead surrendered to Parabrahma, time cannot carry him off. For:

_Trikaaladarshi dinamaan, kalo jagadrakshaka: ||2||_
(Time, the shower of the three times, bright like the sun — time devours the world.)

Commentary: Time comes three times a day to look upon the jivatmas subject to it. For this reason the three periods of time — morning, midday, and evening — are fixed. At these times the influence of time is stronger. In the third shloka the words ‘kalo jagadbhakshaka:’ (time, the devourer of the world) occur; these words are found in the 13th shloka of the Shiva Purana's Kshamapan Stotra.

_Ayurnashyati pashyatam pratidinam yaati kshayam yauvanam |
Pratyaayanti gata: punarna divasa: kalo jagadrakshaka: ||
Lakshmistoyatarangabhangachapala vidyuchchalam jeevitam |
Tasmanmam sharanagatam sharanad tvam raksha rakshadhuna ||13||_
(Meaning: See how, day by day, our lifespan is being destroyed, and our youth is wasting away; the days that have passed do not return. Thus time, in this way, is the devourer of the world. Wealth and riches too, like the ripples of water, are fickle and quick to slip away; and life passes swiftly, like a flash of lightning. Therefore, O Lord who grants refuge to those who take refuge in You, protect me — protect me now, at this very time.)

There is a riddle: a creature walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening — the answer is man. As a child he crawls on four legs; grown up, he walks on two legs; and when he becomes old, he walks with a stick, which becomes his third leg. This condition comes to be understood by us in three ways. Here is Baba Kabirji's couplet.

_Kabir joothe sukhkun sukh kahe, kachhu maanat hai man mod |
E jagat chaveno kaalkun, kachhu mukhman kachhu god ||3||_
(Kabir says: when one calls false pleasure true happiness, the mind takes some delight in it; this world is but a morsel being chewed by time — some souls are already in its mouth, some still lie in its lap, waiting.)

_Kabir mali aavat dekh, kare kali kari pokaar ||
Phoole phoole chun liye, kaal hamaari baahar ||4||_
(Kabir says: seeing the gardener approaching, the still-closed bud cries out in alarm, thinking that the gardener has already picked all the open flowers one by one, while time has passed it by.)

That is to say: Kabirji says that when the soul takes false pleasure to be true happiness, it becomes a morsel devoured by destruction in the form of time (as in Gita, ch. 11, verses 26–32: ‘Kalo'smi lokakshayapravriddho’ — ‘I am time, grown mighty for the destruction of the world’). Thus some have already become morsels in the mouth of time, while others are still kept waiting in its lap to be made into morsels later. The reason for this lies in the subtle ego residing in the mind. As long as one does not abandon this false ego and go for refuge to Parabrahma, one remains subject to time.

Further, Kabirji says that seeing the gardener, in the form of time, coming, the buds of the flower-plant, the jivatmas, that have not yet bloomed cry out in alarm: ‘Today we have not bloomed, but tomorrow we shall bloom — and then this gardener will pick us too.’ By that time, he has already picked all the flowers. Time carries off their lives and departs. Seeing the aged dying, the young too understand that such a turn will come to them as well.

There, the word from Sarvang Leela: from the very beginning, the immobile and the mobile, all creation, have been placed upon time's dining-plate.

_Sakal bhoot aade dei, syavar jangam thaal ||
Ram sanehi baaher, to baante khaay kaal ||5||_
(Placing all beings from the very beginning upon the plate — the immobile and the mobile — time, apportioning them out, devours all except those who are lovingly devoted to Ram.)

That is to say: all beings — past, future, and present, immobile and mobile, gross and inert — insofar as they turn away from devotion to Ram, time devours them in due order. Excepting only those devotees who are lovingly attached to the one Parabrahma ‘Ram,’ time apportions out and devours every other being, each in its turn.

So Shri Vasudev said: ‘O Brahmaji! O Rudradev! Among the whole assembly of gods, including yourselves and others from the beginning, which of them are unable to perform garbhadhyan? Which of them are unable to know their own origin, along with that of the creation? Why is this? Because they remain enveloped all around by Maya (creation). Therefore this world of Maya faces toward time — it is time's food.’ Kabirji speaks a couplet on garbhadhyan:

_Kabir vishva kala ang, vistare lakh chorasi ang ||
Ek eedaman le samye, tab bikaso rahet anang ||6||_
(Kabir says: the whole art and expression of the universe, in all its limbs, expanded into eighty-four lakh forms; when it was drawn together into a single egg, then the limbless one — the bodiless Kamdev, Maya — remained in a state of unfolding.)

_Kabir lakh chorasi naarinar, ek narke ang pehchaan ||
Nitya indu nirmaanmen, bikase seje samaanya ||7||_
(Kabir says: the eighty-four lakh male and female forms are to be recognized as limbs of the one Purusha; within the eternal, ever-forming egg, they unfold gradually, each in its own proper place.)

That is to say: previously, during the time of dissolution, this world lay merged in a dormant state within a single egg called ‘Nara’ (Narayan). From this, the entire expression of the universe expanded, and the eighty-four lakh forms of living beings expanded forth. The four wombs — womb-born, egg-born, sprout-born, and sweat-born — as the places of origin, contain within them the eighty-four lakh bodies, and their development occurs through sexual impulse. All of this comes into being, is created, out of the very limbs of Parabrahma. Along with this, the limbless Kamdev (Kamdev is reckoned to be without limbs) — that is, Maya — also expanded. Here, wherever Kamdev and the like are enumerated, what is being spoken of are the various limbs or aspects of Maya. It is from carnal desire alone that the eighty-four lakh living beings come into being.

Lust, anger, greed, delusion, envy, attachment, aversion, and the like — these are called the limbs of Maya, that is, the gateways through which one slips into Maya.

_Aapo nara iti prokta, aapo vai narasoonava: |
Ta yadasyaayanam poorvam, tena Narayana: smrita: ||7||_ (Manusmriti 1-10)
(The waters are called ‘nara,’ for the waters are the offspring of Nara [Purusha]; and since they were formerly His resting place, He is remembered as Narayan.)

Water is called ‘nar,’ and it was born from ‘Nar’ (the Supreme Being). That water, previously...
